sentence: "She studies public policy, but the policy she criticised yesterday was her own department's." How do the articles distinguish the references?
setupText: Choose the interpretation of the two noun phrases.
taskText: "She studies public policy, but the policy she criticised yesterday was her own department's." How do the articles distinguish the references?
text: Choose the interpretation of the two noun phrases. "She studies public policy, but the policy she criticised yesterday was her own department's." How do the articles distinguish the references?
options: One established policy is contrasted with a new example of the same policy
Two particular policies are contrasted, with identifying details omitted from the first
A field of study is contrasted with a particular departmental course of action
Two fields of study are contrasted, with the second limited to work in one department
answer: A field of study is contrasted with a particular departmental course of action
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-441:Field reference versus a definite individual policy
explanation: Article-free "public policy" names a field. "The policy she criticised" identifies one policy through the following clause. Neither article alone tells us whether the policy has legal force or an international scope.

rationales.A field of study is contrasted with a pa: Bare 'public policy' names the academic field. 'The policy she criticised' identifies one adopted policy through the following clause.
rationales.One established policy is contrasted wit: The first phrase names a field rather than one established policy. The second is definite, not an indefinite introduction of a new example.
rationales.Two particular policies are contrasted,: Studying public policy describes her subject area; it does not establish a first individual policy whose details have been withheld.
rationales.Two fields of study are contrasted, with: The second phrase identifies a policy belonging to a department, not another academic discipline.

sentence: A report says, 'The wealthy were protected from the worst of the losses.' How do the two definite expressions differ?
setupText: Compare the two expressions formed with 'the' plus an adjective.
taskText: A report says, 'The wealthy were protected from the worst of the losses.' How do the two definite expressions differ?
text: Compare the two expressions formed with 'the' plus an adjective. A report says, 'The wealthy were protected from the worst of the losses.' How do the two definite expressions differ?
options: Both expressions denote groups of people, distinguished by their financial circumstances.
The first denotes wealth as a resource; the second identifies the people who lost most of it.
The first denotes wealthy people collectively; the second selects the most severe part of the losses.
Both expressions denote abstract conditions, one favourable and the other unfavourable.
answer: The first denotes wealthy people collectively; the second selects the most severe part of the losses.
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-442:Distinguishing human and abstract reference in the-plus-adjective expressions
explanation: 'The' plus an adjective can denote a human group or an abstract extreme. 'Wealthy' gives the collective people reading; 'worst' is interpreted through the following 'of the losses' phrase.

rationales.Both expressions denote groups of people: 'The wealthy' denotes people, but 'the worst of the losses' selects the most severe part of the losses, not a second human group.
rationales.The first denotes wealthy people collect: 'The' plus an adjective can denote a human group or an abstract extreme. 'Wealthy' gives the collective people reading; 'worst' is interpreted through the following 'of the losses' phrase.
rationales.The first denotes wealth as a resource;: 'Wealthy' describes people possessing wealth, not the resource itself. The losses phrase makes 'worst' refer to losses rather than their sufferers.
rationales.Both expressions denote abstract conditi: 'The wealthy' has plural human reference, reflected in 'were'. Only the second phrase selects an abstract extent of something in this sentence.

sentence: The proposal attracted ___ than its authors had anticipated.
setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
taskText: The proposal attracted ___ than its authors had anticipated.
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. The proposal attracted ___ than its authors had anticipated.
options: good a many more objections
a good much more objections
a good many more objection
a good many more objections
answer: a good many more objections
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-443:Article placement in a good many with a comparative quantity
explanation: "A good many" means quite a large number and takes a plural count noun. Here it modifies the comparison: "a good many more objections".

rationales.a good many more objections: The fixed quantity phrase keeps 'a' before 'good many' and agrees with plural 'objections'.
rationales.good a many more objections: The order of the expression is "a good many", not "good a many".
rationales.a good much more objections: "Objections" is countable and plural; the phrase uses many rather than much.
rationales.a good many more objection: The meaning involves a number of objections, so the noun must be plural.

sentence: "The board approved the merger in principle, subject to agreement on the financing." What does "in principle" contribute?
setupText: Choose the inference supported by the article-free expression.
taskText: "The board approved the merger in principle, subject to agreement on the financing." What does "in principle" contribute?
text: Choose the inference supported by the article-free expression. "The board approved the merger in principle, subject to agreement on the financing." What does "in principle" contribute?
options: Support for the merger's general idea, with financing still an outstanding condition
Support for a broad objective but opposition to this particular proposed merger
Approval of the merger without further conditions, apart from routine financial paperwork
Permission to implement the merger immediately while financing is negotiated afterwards
answer: Support for the merger's general idea, with financing still an outstanding condition
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-444:Article-free in principle as qualified assent
explanation: "In principle" signals assent at the level of the general idea. The financing condition shows that this is not yet unconditional approval of all practical details.

rationales.Support for the merger's general idea, w: In principle grants conceptual approval, while subject to keeps agreement on financing as a condition.
rationales.Support for a broad objective but opposi: The board expresses qualified approval of the merger itself. It does not oppose this proposal while endorsing a different broad objective.
rationales.Approval of the merger without further c: The financing qualification is an unresolved agreement, not merely routine paperwork after unconditional approval.
rationales.Permission to implement the merger immed: The sentence does not authorize implementation before the funding condition is met.

sentence: "A donor offered to fund the restoration. The generosity surprised everyone, but the conditions did not." What identifies "the generosity"?
setupText: Choose the account of the definite reference.
taskText: "A donor offered to fund the restoration. The generosity surprised everyone, but the conditions did not." What identifies "the generosity"?
text: Choose the account of the definite reference. "A donor offered to fund the restoration. The generosity surprised everyone, but the conditions did not." What identifies "the generosity"?
options: A separate charitable act mentioned before the quoted passage
The donor's general character across all previous donations
The total monetary value of every contribution to the project
The quality inferred from the donor's offer in the preceding sentence
answer: The quality inferred from the donor's offer in the preceding sentence
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-445:Definite reference to a quality inferred from an event
explanation: A noun need not have appeared literally before for definite reference to work. The offer makes a quality of generosity available for reference. The passage does not establish the donor's entire history or the project's total funding.

rationales.The quality inferred from the donor's of: The reader derives the quality from the event and can then identify it with the.
rationales.A separate charitable act mentioned befo: The immediately preceding offer supplies the needed connection; no separate act is required.
rationales.The donor's general character across all: The passage supports a quality displayed in this offer, not a general biography of the donor.
rationales.The total monetary value of every contri: 'Generosity' names an evaluated quality here, not the sum of all contributions.

sentence: "The laboratory performs analysis; this particular procedure is an analysis of trace metals." What does "an analysis" present?
setupText: Choose the meaning of the article change.
taskText: "The laboratory performs analysis; this particular procedure is an analysis of trace metals." What does "an analysis" present?
text: Choose the meaning of the article change. "The laboratory performs analysis; this particular procedure is an analysis of trace metals." What does "an analysis" present?
options: Analytical work in general, without presenting an individual procedure
One particular type or instance of an analytical procedure
The specific analysis already identified by the first use of the noun
A laboratory classified by the kind of analytical service it provides
answer: One particular type or instance of an analytical procedure
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-446:Analysis as activity versus a bounded analytical procedure
explanation: Article-free analysis can name the general activity. "An analysis of trace metals" presents one analytical procedure or instance. The indefinite article does not certify validity or mark prior familiarity.

rationales.One particular type or instance of an an: The indefinite article packages the activity as an individual procedure of the specified kind.
rationales.Analytical work in general, without pres: That describes the article-free activity reading in the first clause, not the counted use 'an analysis of trace metals'.
rationales.The specific analysis already identified: The first clause names analysis as an activity; it does not identify an individual procedure for a definite phrase to refer back to.
rationales.A laboratory classified by the kind of a: The second clause classifies the procedure, not the laboratory. Its subject is this particular procedure.

sentence: 'This is not the Alex I remember from university.' What does 'the Alex I remember' identify?
setupText: Alex once avoided crowds; now he hosts huge parties. An old friend comments on the change.
taskText: 'This is not the Alex I remember from university.' What does 'the Alex I remember' identify?
text: Alex once avoided crowds; now he hosts huge parties. An old friend comments on the change. 'This is not the Alex I remember from university.' What does 'the Alex I remember' identify?
options: Another university friend who happened to have the same name
Alex as the person with his former habits and character
Alex as the only person in his university class with that name
Alex as a representative of everyone the speaker knew at university
answer: Alex as the person with his former habits and character
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-447:The with a modified personal name referring to a remembered aspect
explanation: The article and following clause select Alex as remembered by the speaker. A personal name can take 'the' when the phrase identifies a particular version, aspect, or namesake; this context favours a remembered version.

rationales.Another university friend who happened t: The context explicitly concerns a change in Alex's behaviour, not confusion between two people named Alex.
rationales.Alex as the person with his former habit: The article and relative clause select the version of Alex preserved in the speaker's memory.
rationales.Alex as the only person in his universit: The definite phrase identifies a remembered version of him; it supplies no information about classmates' names.
rationales.Alex as a representative of everyone the: The clause identifies the speaker's memory of this individual. It does not make Alex a type representing an entire group.

sentence: "They elected her chair, but she continued to work as a researcher." Why is the first role bare while the second has "a"?
setupText: Choose the interpretation of the article pattern.
taskText: "They elected her chair, but she continued to work as a researcher." Why is the first role bare while the second has "a"?
text: Choose the interpretation of the article pattern. "They elected her chair, but she continued to work as a researcher." Why is the first role bare while the second has "a"?
options: The first is bare because her identity is known; the second is indefinite because her identity is unknown
The first role is uniquely held, so bare chair would also be required after interviewed
The first names an office conferred; the second classifies her continuing professional work
The second article counts a separate research project rather than classifying the person
answer: The first names an office conferred; the second classifies her continuing professional work
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-448:Bare elected office contrasted with indefinite professional classification
explanation: After elect, a role complement can be bare: "elected her chair". "As a researcher" classifies her continuing professional activity. The article patterns do not establish pay or permanence.

rationales.The first names an office conferred; the: Elect licenses the bare role complement, while as a researcher gives an indefinite professional classification.
rationales.The first is bare because her identity i: The same known person is described in both clauses. The difference is in construction and role, not knowledge of her identity.
rationales.The first role is uniquely held, so bare: Interviewed does not license the same role complement: "They interviewed the chair" normally needs a determiner.
rationales.The second article counts a separate res: The noun 'researcher' denotes a person, so the article classifies her professional role rather than counting projects.

sentence: "A certain Mr Bell has been asking to see you." What does "a certain Mr Bell" most naturally do?
setupText: Choose the implication of the introductory phrase.
taskText: "A certain Mr Bell has been asking to see you." What does "a certain Mr Bell" most naturally do?
text: Choose the implication of the introductory phrase. "A certain Mr Bell has been asking to see you." What does "a certain Mr Bell" most naturally do?
options: Identifies a visitor the listener is expected to recognise as the only relevant Bell
Presents Bell as an example of a familiar personality type rather than an individual
Introduces a named visitor without assuming shared familiarity with him
Expresses uncertainty about the surname while affirming familiarity with the person
answer: Introduces a named visitor without assuming shared familiarity with him
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-449:A certain introducing a named but not mutually identified person
explanation: "A certain" can introduce a person by name while leaving their identity or relevance unsettled for the listener. Certain here does not simply mean confident or reliable.

rationales.Introduces a named visitor without assum: A certain introduces the named individual without treating identification by the listener as settled.
rationales.Identifies a visitor the listener is exp: The indefinite introduction does not assume that shared identification.
rationales.Presents Bell as an example of a familia: The visitor is an actual person asking for a meeting, not a type defined by the name Bell.
rationales.Expresses uncertainty about the surname: The construction does not itself cast doubt on the name; it marks how the individual is being introduced.

sentence: Which sentence is correct?
setupText: Choose the grammatically correct version in formal prose.
taskText: Which sentence is correct?
text: Choose the grammatically correct version in formal prose. Which sentence is correct?
options: Rarely have we encountered so compelling an argument.
Rarely have we encountered so a compelling argument.
Rarely have we encountered such compelling an argument.
Rarely have we encountered a so compelling argument.
answer: Rarely have we encountered so compelling an argument.
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-450:Article position in so plus adjective plus singular noun
explanation: In the formal pattern "so + adjective + a/an + singular noun", the adjective precedes the article: "so compelling an argument". The article still matches the sound of argument.

rationales.Rarely have we encountered so a compelli: The so-pattern places the adjective before the article: "so compelling an argument".
rationales.Rarely have we encountered such compelli: With such, the normal order is "such a compelling argument"; this mixes the such and so patterns.
rationales.Rarely have we encountered so compelling: This correctly uses the formal so-adjective-article-noun sequence.
rationales.Rarely have we encountered a so compelli: The degree word 'so' cannot occupy this position after the article in the standard construction.

sentence: Which sentence is correct?
setupText: Choose the grammatically correct version of the formal expression.
taskText: Which sentence is correct?
text: Choose the grammatically correct version of the formal expression. Which sentence is correct?
options: Many a promising scheme has failed for lack of maintenance.
Many a promising schemes has failed for lack of maintenance.
Many a promising scheme have failed for lack of maintenance.
A many promising schemes have failed for lack of maintenance.
answer: Many a promising scheme has failed for lack of maintenance.
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-451:Many a with singular noun and agreement
explanation: Many a has a plural meaning but uses a singular count noun and singular verb: 'Many a scheme has failed.' Keep this formal construction distinct from ordinary 'many schemes have failed'.

rationales.Many a promising scheme has failed for l: The formal quantity expression combines the singular scheme with has even though it refers to many cases.
rationales.Many a promising schemes has failed for: After 'many a', use the singular noun 'scheme'. The plural meaning does not license 'schemes' in this pattern.
rationales.Many a promising scheme have failed for: The head noun 'scheme' is grammatically singular in this construction, so its verb is 'has'.
rationales.A many promising schemes have failed for: This mixes two patterns. Use either 'many promising schemes have' or 'many a promising scheme has'; 'a' cannot simply precede 'many' here.

sentence: 'We are still searching for a framework. The framework must accommodate exceptions without treating them as errors.' How should the second sentence be understood?
setupText: Choose the interpretation that follows from the definite phrase.
taskText: 'We are still searching for a framework. The framework must accommodate exceptions without treating them as errors.' How should the second sentence be understood?
text: Choose the interpretation that follows from the definite phrase. 'We are still searching for a framework. The framework must accommodate exceptions without treating them as errors.' How should the second sentence be understood?
options: It describes a framework already selected, while leaving open whether the framework can meet the requirement
It sets a requirement for the framework being sought, without asserting that one has been found
It refers to an earlier unsuccessful framework and describes the feature that the new one should replace
It announces that the search has ended but that the chosen framework still needs to be tested
answer: It sets a requirement for the framework being sought, without asserting that one has been found
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-452:Definite reference to a sought object without asserting successful discovery
explanation: The definite phrase can continue reference to the object of a search. It specifies what the sought framework must be like, without cancelling "still searching" or asserting that one has been found.

rationales.It describes a framework already selecte: Still searching rules out treating the definite article as an announcement of selection. The phrase continues reference to what is being sought.
rationales.It sets a requirement for the framework: 'Must' states the desired property of the sought object. Definite reference can remain within that projected situation.
rationales.It refers to an earlier unsuccessful fra: No earlier failed framework is established. The natural link is back to a framework in the ongoing search.
rationales.It announces that the search has ended b: Changing a to the maintains reference; it does not cancel the statement that the search is continuing.

sentence: "The reform was introduced in the hope that smaller classes would improve participation." Why is "the hope" natural here?
setupText: Choose the account of the fixed phrase.
taskText: "The reform was introduced in the hope that smaller classes would improve participation." Why is "the hope" natural here?
text: Choose the account of the fixed phrase. "The reform was introduced in the hope that smaller classes would improve participation." Why is "the hope" natural here?
options: The following clause specifies the content of the motivating hope
Hope is countable only when the outcome is guaranteed
Any noun immediately before that must take the
The article proves that all participants shared the same expectation
answer: The following clause specifies the content of the motivating hope
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-453:The with the content clause in in the hope that
explanation: "In the hope that" presents a motivating hope and supplies its content in the following clause. It does not promise success or establish that everyone shared the hope.

rationales.The following clause specifies the conte: This explains the content-linked definite phrase in the established expression.
rationales.Hope is countable only when the outcome: Having a hope does not guarantee its fulfilment, and countability is not determined by success.
rationales.Any noun immediately before that must ta: Compare "a claim that surprised us". A following that-clause does not impose the article mechanically.
rationales.The article proves that all participants: The phrase states the motivation for the reform, not a unanimous belief among participants.

sentence: "The diagnosis was unclear, so she sought a second opinion." Why is "a" possible before "second"?
setupText: Choose the interpretation of the indefinite ordinal phrase.
taskText: "The diagnosis was unclear, so she sought a second opinion." Why is "a" possible before "second"?
text: Choose the interpretation of the indefinite ordinal phrase. "The diagnosis was unclear, so she sought a second opinion." Why is "a" possible before "second"?
options: It selects the second opinion from a numbered set already identifiable to the listener
It introduces an additional opinion rather than identifying an established numbered opinion
It introduces another clinician rather than another opinion, regardless of who gives it
It presents the first diagnosis as mistaken and therefore in need of replacement
answer: It introduces an additional opinion rather than identifying an established numbered opinion
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-454:A with an ordinal meaning an additional instance
explanation: Ordinals do not always require the. "A second opinion" introduces another opinion as an additional instance. "The second opinion" would identify an opinion in an established ordered set.

rationales.It selects the second opinion from a num: That would fit the second opinion in an established sequence. A second opinion introduces an additional instance without requiring such a known set.
rationales.It introduces an additional opinion rath: The indefinite ordinal phrase has the additional-instance reading: another opinion beyond the one already obtained.
rationales.It introduces another clinician rather t: The counted noun is 'opinion'. The phrase does not itself identify or count clinicians.
rationales.It presents the first diagnosis as mista: Seeking an additional view does not establish that the original diagnosis is wrong; it may confirm or clarify it.

sentence: The editor changes 'A dodo is extinct' to 'The dodo is extinct' but leaves 'A dodo laid eggs' unchanged. Why is the article changed only in the first example?
setupText: A museum editor is distinguishing statements about an extinct species from statements about its individual members.
taskText: The editor changes 'A dodo is extinct' to 'The dodo is extinct' but leaves 'A dodo laid eggs' unchanged. Why is the article changed only in the first example?
text: A museum editor is distinguishing statements about an extinct species from statements about its individual members. The editor changes 'A dodo is extinct' to 'The dodo is extinct' but leaves 'A dodo laid eggs' unchanged. Why is the article changed only in the first example?
options: Present-tense general statements require the, whereas past-tense general statements require a
The first statement names a previously identified specimen; the second introduces another specimen
The identifies the only extinct species, while a identifies one of several egg-laying species
Extinction concerns the species as a whole; egg-laying can describe a representative member
answer: Extinction concerns the species as a whole; egg-laying can describe a representative member
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-455:Matching generic article reference to kind-level versus member-level predicates
explanation: A generic indefinite singular can describe a typical member, as in 'a dodo laid eggs'. In its literal biological sense, 'extinct' applies to a species, not an individual bird that dies. The definite singular can name that kind: 'the dodo is extinct'. The distinction is not a tense rule.

rationales.Present-tense general statements require: Article choice is not determined by tense: 'a dodo has a beak' is a possible generic statement, while 'the dodo became extinct' names the species in the past tense.
rationales.Extinction concerns the species as a who: The article needs to fit the kind of property being predicated: extinction of a species versus a characteristic of its members.
rationales.The first statement names a previously i: The museum editor is making general statements, and no individual specimens have been introduced. 'Extinct' does not literally mean that one specimen has died.
rationales.The identifies the only extinct species,: The definite article names this species as a kind; it does not claim that no other species is extinct. The indefinite example represents a typical dodo.

sentence: "For a beginner, the restoration work is remarkably assured." What does "a beginner" contribute?
setupText: Choose the interpretation of the fronted expression.
taskText: "For a beginner, the restoration work is remarkably assured." What does "a beginner" contribute?
text: Choose the interpretation of the fronted expression. "For a beginner, the restoration work is remarkably assured." What does "a beginner" contribute?
options: An identified novice whose name the reader already knows
A claim that exactly one beginner contributed to the restoration
A claim that the restorer has never attempted any related task
A comparison standard based on membership of the beginner category
answer: A comparison standard based on membership of the beginner category
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-456:Indefinite category membership setting an evaluative standard
explanation: "For a beginner" frames the evaluation against expectations for someone in that category. The indefinite article classifies; it does not count all contributors or establish the restorer's complete history.

rationales.An identified novice whose name the read: The phrase supplies a category-based standard, not a name or definite identity.
rationales.A comparison standard based on membershi: This explains how the indefinite phrase qualifies the evaluation of the work.
rationales.A claim that exactly one beginner contri: The article does not state the size or composition of the restoration team.
rationales.A claim that the restorer has never atte: Beginner status does not imply zero related experience.

sentence: "We need research, not a research proposal." What distinction does the article support?
setupText: Choose the account of the contrast.
taskText: "We need research, not a research proposal." What distinction does the article support?
text: Choose the account of the contrast. "We need research, not a research proposal." What distinction does the article support?
options: An informal conversation versus a published scientific result
A completed investigation versus a document that has already been rejected
Several studies versus several proposals
An activity or body of investigation versus one document proposing it
answer: An activity or body of investigation versus one document proposing it
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-457:Article determined by the head noun in a compound noun phrase
explanation: 'Research' is uncountable in the first phrase. In the second, the head noun is countable "proposal", so "a" introduces one document; 'research' modifies the kind of proposal.

rationales.An activity or body of investigation ver: This identifies the head noun and reference type of each phrase.
rationales.An informal conversation versus a publis: The article contrast does not establish informality or publication.
rationales.A completed investigation versus a docum: Research need not be complete, and the proposal's rejection is not stated.
rationales.Several studies versus several proposals: The second phrase is explicitly singular; the first does not supply a count.

sentence: "Not a word of her account was corroborated by the recordings." What does "not a word" convey?
setupText: Choose the interpretation of the negative article phrase.
taskText: "Not a word of her account was corroborated by the recordings." What does "not a word" convey?
text: Choose the interpretation of the negative article phrase. "Not a word of her account was corroborated by the recordings." What does "not a word" convey?
options: One particular word lacked support, while the rest was corroborated
No part of her account received corroboration from those recordings
Her account was conclusively disproved by the recordings
The recordings contained no speech from any participant
answer: No part of her account received corroboration from those recordings
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-458:Emphatic not a minimiser under negation
explanation: "Not a word" is emphatic: even the smallest part of the account received no corroboration from the specified source. Lack of corroboration is not itself proof that the account is false.

rationales.One particular word lacked support, whil: The emphatic phrase denies support throughout the account; it does not isolate one unsupported word.
rationales.No part of her account received corrobor: This preserves both the force of not a and the limited claim about support from the recordings.
rationales.Her account was conclusively disproved b: Not being corroborated is weaker than being disproved. The sentence does not assert conclusive falsification.
rationales.The recordings contained no speech from: The sentence concerns whether the recordings support the account, not whether they contain speech.

sentence: 'She devoted what little free time she had to restoring the archive' becomes 'She devoted a little of her free time to restoring the archive.' Which account preserves the distinction?
setupText: Consider what is lost when an editor changes the quantity phrase.
taskText: 'She devoted what little free time she had to restoring the archive' becomes 'She devoted a little of her free time to restoring the archive.' Which account preserves the distinction?
text: Consider what is lost when an editor changes the quantity phrase. 'She devoted what little free time she had to restoring the archive' becomes 'She devoted a little of her free time to restoring the archive.' Which account preserves the distinction?
options: Both versions say her total free time was scarce; only the revision leaves its use unspecified.
The original presents her available time as plentiful; the revision presents it as scarce.
The original commits her limited supply of free time; the revision states only that she devoted a small amount of it.
The original leaves how much she devoted open; the revision says she devoted her entire small supply.
answer: The original commits her limited supply of free time; the revision states only that she devoted a small amount of it.
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-459:Total limited supply in what little versus an indefinite portion in a little of
explanation: 'What little free time she had' refers to the small total available to her. 'A little of her free time' selects a small amount without saying that this exhausted a limited supply.

rationales.Both versions say her total free time wa: A little of her free time specifies a small amount devoted to restoration, but does not say her total supply of free time was small. Its use is still specified.
rationales.The original presents her available time: 'What little' signals that her available time was limited. The revision quantifies the portion used, not the size of her total supply.
rationales.The original commits her limited supply: 'What little free time she had' refers to the small total available to her. 'A little of her free time' selects a small amount without saying that this exhausted a limited supply.
rationales.The original leaves how much she devoted: This reverses the contrast. The totalising reference belongs to what little she had, not to the partitive a little of her free time.

sentence: A critic dismisses her by saying, 'She is no architect.' Choose the revision that states only her occupational status, without judging the quality of her designs.
setupText: Amira does not practise as an architect, but she sometimes designs useful spaces.
taskText: A critic dismisses her by saying, 'She is no architect.' Choose the revision that states only her occupational status, without judging the quality of her designs.
text: Amira does not practise as an architect, but she sometimes designs useful spaces. A critic dismisses her by saying, 'She is no architect.' Choose the revision that states only her occupational status, without judging the quality of her designs.
options: She is not an architect.
She is not much of an architect.
She is not the architect.
She is no great architect.
answer: She is not an architect.
focusKey: coverage-articles-c1-460:Neutral not a classification versus evaluative no and identifying not the
explanation: Not an architect neutrally denies membership of the professional category. In the critic's dismissive use, no architect suggests that she lacks an architect's competence. The revision removes that evaluation without introducing a particular architect's identity.

Not much of evaluates how good she is at the role; it retains the criticism the revision is meant to remove.
The points to a particular architect relevant to a project or conversation. Denying that identity does not deny being an architect professionally.
The indefinite noun phrase names the professional category; ordinary negation denies that category membership without rating her design skill.
This denies distinction or excellence, not professional status. It can describe someone who is an architect but not a great one.
